We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

At High effort, Fable 5.2 scores about the same as Opus 5.5’s best score (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task, and ahead of GPT-6 Astra’s best score (42.8%) at about the same cost. At Xhigh effort, Fable 5.2 reaches 49.1%, the highest score of any released model we’ve tested.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

Key Takeaways
Claude Fable 5.2 coordinated more than 1,000 agents to build a working operating system in eight days.
The model designed three functional electronic devices, including a voice-assistant hub and USB speakerphone.
Fable 5.2 achieved a 64.9% success rate on the RoboDojo robotics benchmark, outperforming several competing models.
Anthropic’s newest Claude models have taken on engineering challenges that typically demand extensive human expertise and months of work. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have demonstrated significant improvements across software development, robotics, mathematics, and theoretical physics.
During internal testing, Fable 5.2 coordinated more than 1,000 agents to build a working operating system. The model also helped researchers tackle two previously unresolved problems involving black holes. In another experiment, it completed a computer-verifiable formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem in just 30 hours.
These results suggest the models can handle increasingly complex technical assignments. Anthropic says both versions share the same underlying architecture. However, Mythos targets vetted cybersecurity and biomedical research organizations.
Working operating system
One of the more striking experiments involved building an operating system from scratch. An Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 a basic prompt and an empty project folder.
The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days. They wrote code, tested components, and reviewed their work throughout the process.
The resulting operating system could boot on a laptop. It included its own kernel, hardware drivers, and permanent file storage. It also featured a graphical interface, login screen, installer, and built-in Claude functionality.

Software engineering wasn’t the only area where Fable 5.2 demonstrated its capabilities. Anthropic also tasked it with designing three electronic devices.
These included a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The model selected components from US distributors and designed circuit boards. It also created 3D-printed enclosures and wrote the required software.
All three devices worked without electrical modifications. Their circuit boards reached manufacturing readiness in less than a day.
Anthropic also reported a striking result from an internal software migration. A team of agents moved a critical production service from Python to Rust. The resulting service now starts approximately 26 times faster.
Stronger robotics and security
Fable 5.2 also demonstrated substantial improvements in controlling physical robots. On the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieved a 64.9 percent success rate.
That represents a significant jump from Fable 5.1’s 27.6 percent score. It also outperformed GPT-6 Astra, which recorded 29.8 percent on the same evaluation. Opus 5.5 reached 39.4 percent.
The benchmark tests how models control a simulated two-arm robot using camera images. Demonstrations included solving puzzle cubes, opening bottle caps, and drawing pictures.
Cybersecurity results offered another notable performance gain. Anthropic’s specialized Mythos 5.2 model achieved an 89.6% score on its CVE Rediscovery evaluation.
That represents a 10.2 percent improvement over Opus 5.5. It also marks an 11.3 percentage-point increase over Mythos 5.1, which scored 78.3 percent.
A separate security company found that other tested frontier models missed one in six confirmed vulnerabilities identified by Mythos 5.2.
Faster performance, fewer blocks
Anthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than their predecessors. Their standard pricing also starts at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
An optional fast mode increases token generation speeds by up to 2.5 times. However, it doubles the standard pricing.
The company also reports improvements to its safety classifiers. Fable 5.2 produces approximately 55 percent fewer unnecessary blocks than Fable 5.1. Cybersecurity-related blocks fell by 60 percent, while biology-related blocks declined by 40 percent.
These changes should make the models less restrictive during legitimate work. Mythos 5.2, however, remains available only to vetted organizations pursuing approved cybersecurity and biomedical research.

➤ 8 points behind Muse Wonder for about 1/50th of the Cost per Task. Muse Wonder (max) scores 44 at $6.95 per Intelligence Index task
➤ Stands out on AutomationBench-AA. Muse Ember (max) scores 68.1% on AutomationBench-AA, level with Muse Wonder (max), and beats Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) on GDP.pdf (22.8% vs 20.8%), but trails it on AA-Briefcase (1521 vs 1574 Elo)

Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.
Koray Kavukcuoglu
SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

In this article
Gemini 4 Hydrogen is available
Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads
Scaling developer and enterprise workflows
Adaptable speed and intelligence across thinking levels
Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search
Designed for safe, dependable execution for scale
Available to everyone today
Last updated November 13, 2026
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.
While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.
Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads
In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.
Scaling developer and enterprise workflows
Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:
Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.
Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena, arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA.
The new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model is thorough and skeptical in a way I haven't seen from past Gemini models. It is really pleasant and surprising! We have been working on a thorny problem for 10 days with frontier models from competitors and the Hydrogen model was able to catch 2 issues with our approach and proposed a fix. Really amazing and efficient.
By Andrew Carr
Chief Scientist and Co-Founder, Cartwheel
Building with Hydrogen made it very easy to build new tools — it combines the performance of a frontier model with speed that makes iteration on tools feel incredibly lightweight.
By Tris Warkentin
Founding Member of Technical Staff, Discovery Loop
Gemini 4 Hydrogen was the most accurate model on the toxicology and safety section of our Antibody Development benchmark, passing 67% of attempts against 37% for the best non-Gemini model, and the fastest Gemini model at about 13 minutes per task. It reasoned like a cautious safety reviewer, weighing the whole clinical picture rather than single data points and choosing conservative assumptions where patient risk was high.
By Joshua Badshah and Dillon Flood
Biologics Development, LatchBio
Across our reasoning and creative evaluation suite, Gemini 4 Hydrogen matched accuracy with 100% format compliance while slashing end-to-end latency by 28% and cutting total token usage by 23%. From solving complex graph and SQL problems up to 2.8× faster to generating rule-compliant voice ad scripts for StanShop, Hydrogen gives our streaming agents the speed, step-by-step verification, and efficiency we need at scale.
By Rahul Singh
Co-Founder & CTO, STAN
Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows.
Web development: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts.

NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition
November 12, 2026
Jensen Huang Resigns
Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO
Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”  
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” 
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

Anthropic sets price range of $70 to $78 in upcoming IPO
Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut.
The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors.
At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, rising from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May.

As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment, following last week’s midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They’re also facing a public market that’s grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases.
CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a “stretch.”
Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX
 went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk’s reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO.
Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company’s book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called frontier models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September. Anthropic said that the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.

It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.

Claude Code’s “Don’t Ask Again” Approvals Leak Passwords and Keys Into Public GitHub Repos
Approving a command with “don’t ask again” saves it, secrets included, to a project file that Apiiro found holding real credentials in 1,122 public copies.
Published on Nov 10, 2026
Written by Alessandro Mascellino
A safety prompt in Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing passwords, keys and tokens in public GitHub repositories, according to research published by Apiiro on Nov. 5.
Before running a shell command, Claude Code asks the developer for approval. Choosing “Yes, and don’t ask again” turns the full command into a standing rule, stored in a project file called .claude/settings.local.json.
Any password or key in that command is stored with it in plain text. The repository has nothing telling git to keep the file private, so it can end up committed alongside the code.
Apiiro counted 104,185 copies of the file on public GitHub, spread across 103,617 repositories. Real secrets turned up in 1,122 of them, 1,379 distinct secrets in total.
Among the 63 affected organizations were student teams, startups, software agencies and a few established vendors. Leaked credentials included production database passwords, 43 SSH logins for public servers, and cloud and AI model keys, the kind of access attackers have hijacked and resold.
Missed by Scanners, Committed by Claude
Popular secret scanners found only some of them. Gitleaks flagged 564 of the 1,122 files and TruffleHog 643, while 215 got past both.
According to Apiiro, the tools are built to spot recognizable key formats. A password that follows PGPASSWORD= or sshpass -p blends into the rest of the command line, so it often goes unflagged.
In many cases Claude put the file in the repository itself. Apiiro traced 1,105 affected repositories and found Claude listed as co-author on a commit that changed the file in 539 of them. The model’s commit instructions steer it away from files such as .env and credentials.json, but they don’t mention its own settings file.
Removing the file later wasn’t enough either. Older versions in git history held 734 secrets, across 509 repositories, that are missing from every current copy.
Anthropic Looks at Built-In Secret Scanning
Boris Cherny, Anthropic’s head of Claude Code, wrote on Hacker News that Claude Code historically “has not done secret scrubbing,” but that the team was “looking into what we can do to prevent this.”
He listed possible fixes, including “making sure auto mode catches this, building in basic secret scanning.” When another commenter pointed out that auto mode could leak secrets the same way when it pauses on a sensitive command, he answered, “good catch.”
Developers had flagged the behavior in GitHub issues as far back as August 2025. According to Apiiro, Anthropic never answered any of them, and three were closed automatically.
Cherny also wrote that Claude Code automatically gitignores the file when it creates it, “so in this case the files were manually created and checked in.” Apiiro countered that the rule goes only into the developer’s global ignore list, not the repository’s own .gitignore. That leaves out folders turned into repositories later and copies cloned onto other machines. Expert Insights has contacted Anthropic for comment.
Apiiro’s advice to developers was to stop git from tracking the file, list it in the repository’s .gitignore and change every credential it has ever contained, because forks and clones hold copies too. It also suggested keeping secrets out of commands altogether by referring to variables such as $DB_URL.
Apiiro treated a credential as real if it followed a known provider format or appeared alongside a public host, and it didn’t check whether any of them worked. In the median affected repository, the file had first been committed 217 days before Nov. 2.

186 Fake AI Domains Redirect Users to ClickFix Lures, Browser Malware, and Search Hijackers
Ravie LakshmananNov 12, 2026
Browser Security / Web Security
Cybersecurity researchers have found that lookalike domains masquerading as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are being used to serve ClickFix-style lures, browser-hijacking malware, and a set of extensions that hijack user searches.
This delivery pattern has been codenamed TypoPrompting by Island.
"AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else," the cybersecurity company said in a report shared with The Hacker News.
In all, the campaign spans 186 bogus domains spanning 27 AI brands, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), Microsoft Copilot, SpaceXAI Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable, and Cursor.
While one category leads to a ClickFix lure that serves a PowerShell command via a fake Cloudflare verification page, the second route takes unsuspecting users to "Security Check" pages that deliver a browser-hijacking malware called Net Guard. The third pathway sends users to a search-hijack extension family with 16 live Chrome Web Store listings and 972,000 declared users.
Some of the AI lookalike domains are listed below -
cloude[.]ai
cluade[.]ai
clsude[.]ai
chatlgpt[.]com
geimini[.]com
notebookklm[.]com
griok[.]com
preplexity[.]ai
deepceek[.]com
elevenlebs[.]io
copiot[.]com
midj0urney[.]org
An analysis of registration records shows that some of these domains, like cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai, were registered as early as July 13, 2023.
The use of parked domains for malware delivery is not new. In December 2025, Infoblox highlighted how domains without a current web page can be monetized to redirect visitors to sites that serve scams and malware after profiling the host and the device they are visiting from.
"When a domain owner opts into direct search, traffic to the domain is sold to advertisers who bid on keywords and traffic characteristics," the DNS threat intelligence firm noted at the time. "In practice, the site visitor is usually funneled through a series of traffic distribution systems (TDSs) operated by third-party advertising platforms, creating a complex web where a legitimate business model is weaponized for abuse."
In the case of the ClickFix route, the parked page initiates a redirect chain that fingerprints the web browser and collects the public IP address before displaying the fake Cloudflare verification page.
Island said the fingerprint gate script spans a broader set of 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, such as Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow, and Microsoft Azure.
These domains serve three types of lures -
Fake verification pages on Windows that are designed to run a clipboard command
Terminal or security updates on macOS that are designed to run a shell command
Archive download pages that instruct users to extract and run an executable
Separately, eight typosquat domains for Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs, and Voice AI lead to fake "Security Check" pages that ultimately deliver Net Guard.
While the app purports to be a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner and matches the MSIX hash for a legitimate app of the same name, it contains capabilities to run attacker-controlled JavaScript, change the default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.
"The download from the 'Security Check' pages is the Microsoft Store app itself, unmodified," Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, told The Hacker News. "It is byte-for-byte identical to Net Guard as Microsoft distributes it, and it carries Microsoft’s own Store signature."
"The hidden browser control comes with every copy, whether installed from the Store or from a typo site, and it switches itself on without asking. It waits until the user stops using the computer, then takes over Chrome's search settings and can run scripts inside the browser, following instructions from the operator's server."
The third route revolves around a lookalike domain for Perplexity ("preplexity[.]ai"), which redirects the browser to a browser extension called Quick Search that's available on the Chrome Web Store.
"The analyzed extension needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions to perform its main action," Island said. "Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com . Searches made through that provider are sent to a third party. In a workplace, those queries can include internal hostnames, customer names and project details."
Quick Search is part of a larger set of 16 extensions, including GPT for Chrome, which has 80,000 users. In all, the extensions collectively have 972,000 users as of November 3, 2026.
"An address one letter away from an AI tool can lead to a very different request," Island said. "As these services become part of everyday work, reaching the right one should be a managed path, not a test of typing accuracy."
(The story was updated after publication to include a response from Island.)

Introducing Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
November 12, 2026
·
19 min read
·
Edge0
releases
Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer.
On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity.
This release addresses those constraints in four ways:
The constraint	What Edge0-145B makes possible
Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware.	A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s.
Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks.	Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show.
A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions.	The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs.
Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence.	Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money.
We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products.
Get the model weights, explore the inference framework, or try the Edge0 App.
How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer
Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power
Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks.
Requirement	Reported Edge0-145B result	What it enables
Memory	29GB peak memory	Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server.
Prompt processing	1,100+ tokens/s prefill	Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins.
Generation	80+ tokens/s decode	Generates faster than a person reads.
Power	Approximately 120W typical power	Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup.
Long tasks	128K–256K context	Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work.
Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware.
On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards.
Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small
Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory.
Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available.
Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability.
Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud.
Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design
We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling.
Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step.
Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model.
Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand.
Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate.
Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing.
Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency.
What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer
Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work.
Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models
Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following:
Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4.
Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3.
Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5.
Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations.

AI-Generated Code and Technical Debt: Is Your Codebase Fragile?
Developers Digest

•
7 min read
AI Agents
Claude Code
Code Review
Engineering
TL;DR
A viral essay argues AI-written code makes codebases fragile: shallow tests, needless complexity, lost understanding, no time to review. What holds up, what is anecdote, and four checks to run on your own repo.
Enjoy the article? Get more like it.
One email per week. Tutorials, open-source projects, and deep dives. Free.
Last updated: November 11, 2026
An essay titled "AI usage generates a fragile codebase" reached the Hacker News front page this week with more than 600 points and nearly 600 comments. If you have been searching for whether AI-generated code adds technical debt, this is the argument in its sharpest form, and the thread around it is a useful reality check. The short version: the claims are anecdotal, but the four failure modes are specific enough to test in your own repository on Monday.
What the primary source says#
The essay by Evan X. Merz (November 7, 2026) is a first-person account. The author says he suspects he was laid off from Meta in May partly because he resisted heavy AI use, even though he generated at least 90% of his code with AI in his last months there. He now works at another large company and generates all of his code with AI because that is the expectation. His claim is not that agents are useless, but that they solve what fits in a context window and are "oblivious" to long-term issues that do not.
He lists four ways AI makes a codebase fragile:
Shallow tests. Agents write many tests of trivial get/set methods, and end-to-end tests that cover only the cases the codebase already handles, such as one type of user. Line coverage hides the gaps.
Overly complex code. Several helper methods where one would do, and rules like DRY followed to a fault.
Less human understanding. The longer agents write the code, the fewer people understand the data structures well enough to spot a new abstraction that clashes with existing ones.
Speed beats the quality bar. Each pull request arrives faster than the last and gets less review time, so small issues pile up.
He then lists four symptoms: more incidents, slower recovery, errors only users see, and a worse user experience. Note what this is: observation from one career, not a study. There are no incident counts or before-and-after numbers in it.
The angle: it is a review-capacity problem wearing a quality costume#
Read closely, three of the four mechanisms are about the same constraint - human attention. Shallow tests, creeping complexity and lost understanding all get through because nobody had the time to catch them. That matches what we have argued before in AI code review is the new bottleneck and coding agents move the bottleneck to review queues: generation got cheap, judgment did not.
Who wins from this framing: teams that spend the saved typing time on tests, plans and review. Who loses: teams that count lines or PRs merged as productivity, because that metric rewards exactly the behavior the essay describes. The second-order effect is that the scarce skill shifts toward knowing what good looks like, which is the case made in domain expertise as the agentic coding moat.
What to do Monday: four checks#
Each check maps to one failure mode and needs no new tooling.
1. Audit the tests an agent wrote. Pick one recent agent-authored feature and ask: if I deleted the core logic, would a test fail for the right reason? Replace line coverage as your success signal with a mutation check on that one module, or simply break the code by hand and see what notices.
2. Find the duplicated rule. A commenter on the thread described an agent that calculated a serialized string length separately from the serializer itself - it worked, but opened a path to a future bug. Grep for places where one business rule is implemented twice. Duplicated policy is cheap for an agent to write and expensive to keep in sync.
3. Look at churn, not just size. Files that change in every PR are where fragility shows up first. This standard git command lists the most-changed files in the last 90 days:
TERMINAL
git log --since="90 days ago" --name-only --pretty=format: | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
Read the top three with a human eye. If an abstraction there looks generic but is used once, it is a candidate to simplify.
4. Put the plan before the code. One commenter described the workflow that worked for them: have the agent draft a plan in a file, add inline comments, have the same session process them, repeat until the plan is detailed, and only then give the go signal. That moves review to the cheapest moment. Our guide to Claude Code review levels covers how to match review depth to risk.
What people are actually saying#
The Hacker News discussion splits roughly three ways.
Agreement from experience. Several commenters described agents overfitting: a fix that works only because of the current state of several unrelated files, and breaks when any of them change. Another described a request for a small alerting plumbing change that came back as 400 lines hard-coded for one metric, so a second alert would need another 400.
The business counter-case. A 20-year engineer who now writes all code with AI argued that enterprise code was rarely about robustness anyway, and that quality was always something engineers defended against business pressure. In this view the essay describes an old problem accelerated, not a new one.
Skepticism of both sides. Some pointed out that many pro-AI comments come from brand-new accounts, others that the opposing camp has its own incentives. One commenter said the most productive thing they had done was shrink their codebase, and another noted LLMs may work better on concrete code with fewer abstraction layers - the opposite of adding more structure.
Take the strongest counter-case seriously: the essay offers no measurements, the author's own employer mandates AI use, and survivorship runs both ways. A team with strong tests and review discipline may see none of these symptoms.
FAQ#
Does AI-generated code create more technical debt?#
The essay says so and names four mechanisms, but it is experience, not data. The mechanisms are plausible and checkable.
How do I tell if agents are hurting my codebase?#
Compare incident count, recovery time and user-only errors before and after your team moved to agent-written code, and audit the tests agents wrote.
Should teams stop using coding agents?#
No. The author uses them for all his code. Put guardrails where the failure modes are: test quality, diff size, written plans and review time.
